title: Save and share with Git and GitHub

explanation.text: This lesson is for your own PC, so the commands have a **Copy** button and no Run button.

**Git** is a tool that keeps the history of your project. Each saved step is a **commit**: a snapshot with a short message. You can look back and undo mistakes. **GitHub** is a website that stores a copy of your project online, so you can share it and show it in your portfolio.

items: Install Git (from git-scm.com) and make a free GitHub account.
Check the install: run `git --version` in a terminal.
Use only code, fake data and notes that you are happy for the world to see, if the repository is public.

explanation.title: first-time setup
explanation.text: Run these once on your PC. Use your own name and email.
explanation.code:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

explanation.title: save your project (your first commit)
explanation.text: Run these inside your project folder. "git status" shows what changed, so use it often.
explanation.code:
git init
git add .
git status
git commit -m "Add customer list cleaner and README"

explanation.title: .gitignore file
explanation.text: Make a file named .gitignore in your project folder, then add it BEFORE the first "git add ." so these files are never saved. Add the names of your own private files.

explanation.title: put it on GitHub
explanation.text: First make a new empty repository on github.com (do not tick "add a README"). Copy its address and put it in the second line.
explanation.code:
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-NAME/YOUR-REPO.git
git push -u origin main

explanation.title: the everyday loop
explanation.text: After a change that works, save it and send it.
explanation.code:
git add .
git commit -m "Handle empty lines in the input file"
git push

explanation.text: Commit messages tell the story of your project. Write what changed, in plain words: "Fix crash on empty file" is much better than "update".
**Never commit keys, passwords or real private data.** If you do by mistake, change the key at once. Deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from the history.

examples.title: Weak and better commit messages
examples.code:
Weak: "update"
Weak: "stuff"
Better: "Add report with totals per customer"
Better: "Fix crash when the input file is empty"

examples.title: What belongs in the repository
examples.code:
Yes: your code, the README, small fake sample files, .gitignore.
No: API keys, passwords, real customer files, big downloaded data, the venv folder.

quiz.question: What is a commit?
options: A saved snapshot of your project with a message
quiz.explanation: A commit is one step in the history of your project, with a short message that says what changed.

quiz.question: Which file should NOT be committed?
options: A file with your API key
quiz.explanation: Secrets must stay out of the repository, especially a public one.

quiz.question: What does GitHub give you?
options: A place to store and share your project online
quiz.explanation: GitHub keeps an online copy of your repository, so you can share it and show it to others.
